summary.text: For even \(m\ge 8\), apply positivity at the odd integer \(n=m-1\); a witness prime \(p\) has lower companion \(n-(p-1)=m-p\), giving Goldbach, while \(m=4,6\) are handled directly. For odd \(m\ge 9\), apply it at the even integer \(n=m-1\); a witness prime \(q\) has lower companion \(n-(2q-1)=m-2q\), giving Lemoine, with \(m=7\) handled directly.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)=A261627(n)\) be defined as follows. Put
\[
\varepsilon(n)=
\begin{cases}
1,&n\text{ odd},\\
2,&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(a(n)\) is the number of primes \(p<n+1\) for which, on setting
\[
d=p\varepsilon(n)-1,
\]
one has \(d<n\) and both \(n-d\) and \(n+d\) prime. The inequality \(d<n\) ensures that the subtraction \(n-d\) is ordinary nonnegative integer subtraction.

Assume the main A261627 conjecture:
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>6.
\]
We prove from this assumption both the strong Goldbach conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.

First record the direct consequence of positivity that will be used twice. If \(n>6\), then \(a(n)>0\), so the finite set counted by \(a(n)\) is nonempty. Hence there is a prime \(p<n+1\) such that, with \(d=p\varepsilon(n)-1\),
\[
d<n,\qquad n-d\text{ is prime},\qquad n+d\text{ is prime}.
\]
Only the primality of \(p\) and \(n-d\), together with \(d<n\), will be needed below; the extra condition that \(n+d\) is prime is part of the stronger A261627 hypothesis but is not needed for either consequence.

## Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(m\ge 4\) be even. We must exhibit primes whose sum is \(m\).

There are three cases. If \(m=4\), then
\[
4=2+2,
\]
and both summands are prime. If \(m=6\), then
\[
6=3+3,
\]
and again both summands are prime.

It remains to consider an even \(m\ge 8\). Set
\[
n=m-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge 7\), so \(n>6\), and because \(m\) is even, \(n\) is odd. Consequently \(\varepsilon(n)=1\). By the assumed positivity of \(a(n)\), choose a prime \(p\) satisfying the A261627 conditions. In the present odd case,
\[
d=p\varepsilon(n)-1=p-1.
\]
Thus
\[
p-1<n
\]
and
\[
r:=n-(p-1)
\]
is prime.

We claim that \(m=p+r\). Since \(p-1<n\), in particular \(p-1\le n\), so subtraction has no truncation and
\[
n=(p-1)+\bigl(n-(p-1)\bigr)=(p-1)+r.
\]
Adding \(1\) gives
\[
m=n+1=(p-1)+r+1=p+r.
\]
Both \(p\) and \(r\) are prime, so this is the required Goldbach representation.

These cases exhaust all even integers at least \(4\): after \(4\) and \(6\), the next possible even integer is \(8\). Therefore every even \(m\ge4\) is a sum of two primes, proving the strong Goldbach conjecture.

## Lemoine's conjecture

Now let \(m\ge7\) be odd. We must exhibit primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
m=p+2q.
\]

If \(m=7\), take \(p=3\) and \(q=2\). Both are prime, and
\[
7=3+2\cdot2.
\]

Suppose now that \(m\ne7\). Since \(m\) is odd and at least \(7\), the next possibility after \(7\) is \(9\); hence \(m\ge9\). Again set
\[
n=m-1.
\]
Then \(n\ge8>6\), and because \(m\) is odd, \(n\) is even. Therefore \(\varepsilon(n)=2\). Positivity of \(a(n)\) supplies a prime \(q\) satisfying the A261627 conditions. In this even case the associated displacement is
\[
d=q\varepsilon(n)-1=2q-1.
\]
We therefore have
\[
2q-1<n
\]
and
\[
r:=n-(2q-1)
\]
is prime.

As before, the strict inequality \(2q-1<n\) implies \(2q-1\le n\), so the subtraction is exact and
\[
n=(2q-1)+\bigl(n-(2q-1)\bigr)=(2q-1)+r.
\]
Adding \(1\) yields
\[
m=n+1=(2q-1)+r+1=2q+r=r+2q.
\]
Thus, taking \(p=r\), both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime and \(m=p+2q\), as required.

The case \(m=7\) and the case \(m\ge9\) exhaust all odd integers at least \(7\). Hence every odd integer at least \(7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, proving Lemoine's conjecture.

We have therefore shown that the assertion \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>6\) implies both Goldbach's conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.
